newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Sacred cows at risk as UK reviews defence.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sacred cows at risk as UK reviews defence.

text.p: London's corridors of government are filled with the sound of sacred cows facing the prospect of slaughter as Britain starts to review its defence needs for the next 20 years.

The new Labour government has made clear that nothing is sacrosanct and some of the questions being asked in the defence review could trigger apoplexy in those who take it for granted that Britain should sit at the top table.

Does Britain really need such a close relationship with the United States? Why does it need nuclear weapons? Why doesn't it focus on Europe and ditch any pretensions of playing a role on the world stage?
Perhaps most unusually of all, Labour is reaching beyond the traditionally closed circle of policy makers to canvass outsiders for their views.
In an unprecendented move, ministers and senior officials held the first of two open seminars in early July to pick the brains of defence experts, international affairs analysts and journalists.

"We want the input and inspiration of those outside government. The outcome will be stronger and healthier. We want to challenge received wisdom," Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said at the start of the four-hour session.
POST COLD-WAR RETHINK

Cook's presence reflected the government's belief that future defence requirements are inextricably linked to a foreign policy which also needs to be rethought in the wake of the Cold War and appearance of new threats.
"Now we are casting our minds forward to 2015, to how our policies and principles will be relevant and what we can do to change to best secure the security of the British people," he said.
It was all much easier in the days of long-lived 19th century monarch Queen Victoria, whose initials dot the gilded splendour of the Foreign Office's Locarno Room, where the seminar took place.

But simply sending in a gunboat or an army or two to quell trouble in some distant dusty corner of the empire is no longer an option in the days when budgets are tight and a whole host of new threats has emerged.
"We are left with a serious dilemma. Our experience of war so far is one country attacking the other. What is happening now is the emergence of intra-state conflicts," Cook said.
"We have been appallingly slow at developing ways of combating this. We must build an international response to these threats."
DANGER FROM DISTANT CONFLICTS

The Afghan civil war was a good example of how a distant conflict could endanger Britain, he said, since 80 percent of the heroin trafficked in London was grown in or exported through Afghanistan. Guerrilla movements hostile to the west also posed a growing risk.
"What is the best balance between preventing terrorism in Britain and solving long-standing conflicts which have exported that terrorism to the west?" Cook asked.
Jeremy Greenstock, head of foreign policy at the Foreign Office, posed questions which in earlier times might have resulted in execution for treason.
"Should Britain have a global reach in diplomacy as the world changes?"
"How intensive should diplomatic involvement be in the world? Can Britain have a leading role in the United Nations, NATO, the European Union and the Commonwealth?"
Some questioned the need for a costly conventional army, air force and navy stretching across the world when Britain's empire had all but crumbled away and the main dangers were closer to home.

"Britain needs European security. We must do what we can to increase European security and interlock as much of Europe as possible into interdependent structures," said Sir Timothy Garden, head of the Royal Institute for International Affairs think-tank.
Richard Hatfield, deputy under secretary of policy at the defence ministry, said Britain did not face a serious external threat in the short or the medium term.

"There is no doubt that the major threat to British security comes from Northern Ireland terrorism. Countering it remains a large military task," he said, adding that other possible risks included an unstable Russia and problems in southeastern Europe and the Gulf.
DANGER OF UPHEAVAL IN MIDDLE EAST
Lord William Wallace, a reader in international relations at the London School of Economics, said Britain should keep its eye firmly on the Middle East.

"We've been arming countries round the Gulf and the probability is that one regime there will collapse in the next five years -- possibly Saudi Arabia -- and Europe has to figure out how to deal with it," he said.
Defence Secretary George Robertson made clear that some cornerstones would remain in place.
"Cooperation with the United States and like-minded allies will continue. We will rely on NATO, but there is no reason why it can't be changed," he said.
BBC World Service defence correspondent Mark Laity urged against a radical reorganisation and surrender to those clamouring for a lower defence budget.
"There are very few countries which have any kind of global reach at any level," he asked.
"We pay for competence -- there are a lot of not very good armies out there. For us to drop our punch is to leave it to someone else, but who else is out there?"
Cook took up the theme as he wrapped up the debate.
"I do think it would be paradoxical, given the shrinking of the globe, to see the sphere of our interests diminished," he said.
"But this doesn't mean we have to have a military presence on all four quarters of the globe."
